questions.question: Why can a simple optimal-path plan still be unsuitable for a VR tour in a very large virtual environment?
options: It may make the user move faster than natural walking speed.
Its shortest tour covering all points of interest may still exceed a safe exposure time.
It may set an upper limit on how long the user can stay exposed.
It may cover only the most important points of interest.
questions.explanation: The optimal path approach can still require a very large amount of time even in minimum time, and long VR exposure can lead to cybersickness.

questions.question: What is the goal of an optimal path under a time constraint in VR navigation?
options: To select points based only on their Euclidean distance from one another.
To visit every point of interest in the shortest possible time.
To choose a route that avoids interacting with any point of interest.
To cover as many important points of interest as possible within a set exposure limit.
questions.explanation: The time-constrained approach sets an upper time limit and then finds a path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest.

questions.question: In the time-constrained VR navigation approach, what does covering a point of interest include?
options: Only following the shortest Euclidean edge to the next point.
Only looking at a picture of the point before continuing.
Interacting with or inspecting the point and moving between points.
Only reaching the point's location without stopping.
questions.explanation: Covering a point of interest includes interacting with or inspecting it and navigating from one point to another.

questions.question: Why is a full-day walking exploration of Auniati Satra discouraged as a VR tour?
options: It would require users to walk faster than their natural speed.
It would make it impossible to model the campus as a graph.
Full-day exposure to a VR tour can induce cybersickness.
It would prevent the tour from including any cultural aspects.
questions.explanation: Exploring the whole Satra by walking may take up to a day, and a full-day VR exposure is not recommended because it would induce cybersickness.

questions.question: In the graph model of the Satra campus, what do the nodes represent and how are edge weights defined?
options: Nodes are scene-graph objects, and edge weights are rendering priorities.
Nodes are points of interest, and edge weights are Euclidean distances between them.
Nodes are user categories, and edge weights are waiting times.
Nodes are physical objects, and edge weights are shortest walking times.
questions.explanation: The Satra campus graph uses points of interest as nodes and weights edges by the Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest.

questions.question: How was the data for the Satra graph collected?
options: By recording travel automatically with wearable sensors and interviewing only tourists.
By running a TSP solver over a satellite map to identify likely stopping places.
By listing all objects in a scene graph and asking residents to assign importance values.
By observing travel and stopping behavior and interviewing residents and Satra committee members.
questions.explanation: The field study observed people's travel and stopping behavior and interviewed campus residents and Satra committee members.

questions.question: What is true about points of interest in the Satra graph?
options: They must be nodes in the scene graph of the virtual environment.
They must be one of the 22 Satras on Majuli.
They must be tangible objects that visitors can physically interact with.
They do not have to be actual physical objects; a lake's corners can be points of interest.
questions.explanation: A point of interest need not refer to an actual physical object; the lake itself is not treated as a point of interest, but its corners are.

questions.question: What does the maximum wait time at a point of interest include?
options: Only the time spent looking at the point of interest.
The time needed to travel from one point of interest to the next.
Stopping, inspecting, interacting if possible, and resuming navigation.
The total time available for the whole virtual tour.
questions.explanation: Maximum wait time is the time needed to stop at the point of interest, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation.

questions.question: Which solver is used to find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the most important points of interest while accounting for wait times?
options: A scene-graph optimizer.
A vehicle routing problem with profits solver.
A traveling salesman problem solver.
A neuron-interconnection solver.
questions.explanation: Once the graph is available, a VRPP solver can find a path within a time threshold that covers the maximum number of most important points of interest while accounting for wait times.

questions.question: Why can a virtual reality navigation path that minimizes total time to visit every point of interest in Auniati Satra still be unsuitable for a user, and what does the time-constrained path choose instead?
questions.reference_answer: In a very large virtual world, the minimum time to explore all points of interest may still be very large compared with expected user exposure duration, so it may lead to cybersickness. Exploring the whole Auniati Satra by walking can take up to a day, and a full-day VR exposure is not recommended because it would induce cybersickness. The optimal path under a time constraint approach sets an upper time limit, the time threshold, and within that duration it selects a path that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest, including interacting, inspecting, and navigating between them.

questions.question: What kinds of information must be captured when converting the Auniati Satra site into a graph for navigation optimization, and why can field study influence which locations become nodes?
questions.reference_answer: The graph represents points of interest as nodes, with at least 25 nodes for the Satra campus, and edges between pairs of nodes are weighted by Euclidean distance between the corresponding points of interest. Converting the site into a graph is iterative and requires detailed field study and revision. The field study is a contextual inquiry in which people’s travel and stopping behavior are observed and recorded, and residents and Satra committee members are interviewed about typical places and recommended places. A point of interest does not have to be a physical object; for example, a lake is not treated as a point of interest, but the corners of the lake are.

questions.question: How do a traveling salesman problem solver and a vehicle routing problem with profit solver support different virtual tour goals for Auniati Satra, and what additional information does the vehicle routing problem with profit approach require from the graph nodes?
questions.reference_answer: A TSP solver can find a minimum-time path that covers all 25 nodes, while a VRPP solver can find a path within a chosen time threshold that covers the maximum number of the most important points of interest. VRPP treats the importance of nodes as profit and allows not all nodes to be visited within the time constraint. For this second approach, each point of interest needs a relative importance from discussions and an estimated maximum wait time from observed visitor behavior. The maximum wait time is the time a user needs to stop at the point, inspect it, interact with it if possible, and resume navigation.
